parole.significato: Forms agent nouns, mostly from verbs of Romance or Latin origin.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -ant, from Latin -ans, -antis, in part through Old French -ant.

parole.significato: Used to form verbal nouns, which often have an informal, frequentative and/or negative overtone.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -erīe, from Old French -erie. The suffix first became productive in German to designate workshops pertaining to occupation names ending in -er, such as Bäckerei (“bakery”) from Bäcker (“baker”). These cases are more properly analyzed as derivations in -ei from the occupation

parole.significato: Verb suffix: it and its inflected forms are found mainly as a rendering of French, Italian, and Latin suffixes like -ir…
parole.testo: From Middle High German -ieren, extracted by rebracketing of verbs borrowed from (Old) French, such as parlieren (Old French parlier + -en), or Italian, such as spazieren (Italian spaziare + -en).
Compromise form between Middle High German -itēt, from Old French -ite(t), and older -itāt, directly from Latin -itās.

parole.significato: Suffix added to numerals and pronouns to create determiners/pronouns indicating variety
parole.testo: From Middle High German lei f (“kind”), from Old French lei, from Latin lex. Cognate with Dutch -lei.
From Middle High German âventiure, borrowed from Old French aventure and like the latter originally feminine. The neuter gender is from Middle Low German.
From Middle High German adē, from Old French adieu. Doublet of tschö.
From Middle High German advocāte (14th c.), from Old French advocat, from Latin advocātus. Doublet of the earlier borrowing Vogt.
From Early New High German axise, accise (16th century), from Middle High German assīse, from Old French assise. Ultimately from Latin assidēre.
Middle High German alūn, Old High German alūne, from Old French alun, from Latin alūmen.
From French allier + -ieren, from Old French alier, from Latin alligāre.

Borrowed from Old French apetit or directly from its source, Late Latin appetītus (“attack; striving, desire; appetite”), a fourth-declension noun derived from Latin appetō (“to assail; to strive after”).

parole.significato: to finish a textile (to improve the look, performance, or feel of a textile or clothing)
parole.testo: From French apprêter + -ieren, from Old French aprester.
From Middle High German barre, from Old French barre.
From Middle High German bastart, basthart (“illegitimate child of a nobleman”), from Old French bastart, probably from Frankish, but the precise derivation is uncertain.
From Middle High German buckel, from Old French boucle, from Latin buccula.

parole.significato: deuce, the number two in German games
parole.testo: From Middle High German dūs, from Old High German dūs, from Old French dous (“two”). Applied on a person possibly the same word, being most frequent in the interjection “Ei der Daus!”, stemming from the deuce, the highest card, being played, and hence having an ambiguous sense depending on the angle
From Middle High German dīemant, dīamant, dīamante, borrowed from Old French diamant.
From Old French dilatation, from Late Latin dīlātātio.
From Old French doble.
From Middle High German tozen via tutzet, dutzet. Derived from Old French dozaine (today douzaine), from doze, from Latin duodecim. Not related to Dutch duizend (“thousand”).

From Middle High German īnvluz, īnfluz, invluz, influz, from Old High German influz, from Old French influence, Latin īnfluēns. By surface analysis, deverbal from einfließen. Also analysable as ein- + Fluss. Compare Middle Low German invlôt, Dutch invloed, English inflood; English inflow.
From Middle High German fabele, from Old French fable, from Latin fabula.

From Middle High German fasān, fasant, alteration after Old French fasan(t) of older fashuon, from Old High German fasihuon, itself an alteration based on huon (“chicken”) of unattested *fasiān, from Latin phasianus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós).

parole.significato: for there to be a lack [with dative ‘to someone/something’ and an (+ dative) ‘of something’] (idiomatically translated…
parole.testo: From Middle High German vælen, velen, valen, from Old French falir, faillir, from Latin fallō. Cognate with English fail.
From Middle High German fīn, from Old French fin, ultimately from Latin finis. See English fine for more.

parole.significato: varnish (clear, hardening protective layer, typically from linseed oil, especially applied to paintings)
parole.testo: From Middle High German firnîs, vernîʒ, from Old French vernis.
Inherited from Middle High German fix, influenced by French fixe.
From Middle High German formieren, from Old French former and Latin fōrmāre. By surface analysis, Form + -ieren.
From Middle High German franc, from Old French franc (“free”), of Germanic but eventually uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Frenchman (person of French birth or nationality)
parole.testo: From Middle High German franzōse, franzoise, from Old French françois.

From Middle High German franzoisisch, franzoisch (franzois, franzoys, franzeis), borrowed from Old French françois + -isch. Analysable as Franzose (“Frenchman”) + -isch. Replaced Middle High German franzisch, from francisc, frenkisc, Old High German frenkisk.

Eventually from Old French guarnir, from Frankish *warnijan (“to ward, take care of”), from Proto-Germanic *warnijaną. Related to but not identical with German warnen, English warn. Perhaps partly through Middle Low German garnēren (“to clad with wood”, 15th c.), but in the contemporary sense (17th

From Middle High German gegende, equivalent to gegen + -de, which is an alteration of older gegenōte, from Old High German geginōti, probably after Old French contree, whence also English country. Compare Dutch jegenode.

parole.significato: grail (holy, miraculous object, especially a cup)
parole.testo: From Middle High German grāl, from Old French graal, from Latin gradalis.

parole.significato: armour covering the torso of a medieval knight
parole.testo: From Middle High German harnasch, harnisch, from Old French hernois. Usually derived from an Old Norse *hernest (“army equipment”), from herr (“army”) + nest (“provisions”) (from Proto-Germanic *nesaną (“to heal, recover”)), the former related with German Heer. A less likely derivation is from Old B
Via Old French from Late Latin hecticus (“febrile”), from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός (hektikós, “habitual”).
14th century, from Middle High German heralt, from Old French héraut and its latinisation Medieval Latin heraldus, from Proto-West Germanic *heriwald. See herald for more.
Middle High German hurteclich, from hurt, from Old French hurt (French heurt).
From French imaginer + -ieren, from Old French imaginer, from Latin imāginor, from Latin imāginem, the accusative singular of Latin imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

parole.significato: to interpret (to explain or tell the meaning of; to apprehend and represent by means of art)
parole.testo: From French interpréter + -ieren, from Old French enterpreter, from Latin interpretor (“to explain, expound, interpret”).
From Old French chan, from Medieval Latin canus, caanus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.

Inherited from Middle High German kolter m or f or n, from Old French coultre (“quilt”), from Vulgar Latin *culcitra, from Latin culcita (“pillow, upholstery, mattress”). Cognate with English quilt and quoit.
From Middle High German comēte, from Old French comete, from Latin comēta.

parole.significato: commander, knight commander (of a basic administrative division called Kommende or Komturei)
parole.testo: Middle High German kumtur, from Old French commendeor, from Medieval Latin commendātor.
Middle High German kunterfeit, from Old French contrefait, Medieval Latin contrafacere.
Borrowed from Old French cople, couple, from Latin copula.
Inherited from Middle High German koppeln, kuppeln, kupelen (“to bind (to a paddock, chiefly dogs); to pinion”), a hunting jargon term borrowed from Old French copler, coupler. Doublet of kuppeln.
From Middle High German koral, from Old French coral, from Latin corallium.
From Middle High German kosten, from Old French coster, from Latin cōnstō.
From Middle High German kotze, from Old High German chozzo, probably from Old French cotte (“overshirt”).

parole.significato: friend in the same business (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kompān, kumpān, from Old French compain (“friend; companion”), from Late Latin compāniō (literally “he with whom one shares one's bread”), from com- + pānis (with + bread).
Inherited from Middle High German koppeln, kuppeln, kupelen (“to bind (to a paddock, chiefly dogs); to pinion”), a hunting jargon term borrowed from Old French copler, coupler. Doublet of koppeln.

parole.significato: to take care, to look after
parole.testo: From Middle High German kumbern, derived from the noun kumber, probably from Old French *combre (“obstruction, barrier”), itself probably from Gaulish. See Kummer for more. Cognate with Hunsrik kimmre, Luxembourgish këmmeren and Dutch kommer.
From Middle High German lakerize, from Old French licorece or directly from Medieval Latin, from Late Latin liquiritia, from Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza, “sweet root”).

parole.significato: lance, spear (weapon used mainly for thrusting)
parole.testo: From Middle High German lanze, borrowed from Old French lance.
From Middle High German lūte (14th c.), from Old French leüt, from Old Spanish laúd, alod, from Arabic اَلْعُود (al-ʕūd).

From Middle High German lieveren (before 1350), which may be borrowed directly from Old French livrer, from Latin līberō, but was probably introduced via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German lēveren (the vocalism -ie- then being due to hypercorrection; compare also attested liebern). Low German defini
From Middle High German maniere, borrowed from Old French maniere, derived from Latin manuārius.
From Middle High German mat, with influence from Old French mat (“in checkmate”), a clipping of French échec et mat (“checkmate”), and French mat (“matt; pale”).

parole.significato: medicine (the study of disease and treatment; the profession based thereon)
parole.testo: From Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna.
Modification of Mostert, from Old French moustarde, from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum (“must; unfermented or partially fermented grape juice or wine”).

From Middle High German muscāt, from Old French muscate, from Medieval Latin (nux) muscāta (“nutmeg”), from muscātus (“musky”), from Late Latin muscus (“musk”), from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos, “musk”).

parole.significato: the main building of a medieval fortified castle, containing the great hall
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Middle High German palas, from Old French palais, pales, from Late Latin palātium. Doublet of Pfalz, Palast, and Palais.

From Middle High German palast (13th c.), enhanced form of older palas (12th c.), from Old French palais, from Latin palātium. Doublet of Pfalz, Palas, and Palais. Stress varied until the 19th century (Pálast or Palást).
From older Banier, from Middle High German banier, baniere, borrowed from Old French baniere, itself from Frankish [Term?]. Doublet of Banner.
From Middle High German panze, from Old French pance (Modern French panse), from Latin pantex (“belly”).
From Ripuarian dialect where it originally meant stomach. From Old French pance, from Latin pantex.

From Middle High German papegei, from Old French papegai, from Old Spanish papagayo, from Byzantine Greek παπαγάς (papagás), from Arabic بَبَّغَاء (babbaḡāʔ). Further origin unknown, perhaps from an African language or imitative. The Middle High German variant papegān may have been borrowed directly

parole.significato: pope (head of the Roman Catholic Church; title of other religious leaders such as the Coptic Pope)
parole.testo: From Middle High German pābest, bābest, from earlier bābes, from Old High German bābes, from Old French pape, from Latin pāpa, pappa (“father”, originally). Doublet of Pfaffe. Forms in B- remained predominant during the 15th and 16th centuries before they were gradually displaced by the more Latin-l

Inherited from Middle High German parlamënt n (“meeting; disputation; assembly”), from Old French parlement (“parliament”), from Middle English parlement (“discussion; parliament”), itself from Old French parlement (“discussion”), from parler (“to speak”) + -ment, from Medieval Latin parabolō (“to s
From Middle High German parlieren, from Old French parlier (“to speak”) + -en.

parole.significato: part; role (that which an actor, singer, or other artist contributes to a performance)
parole.testo: From Middle High German part f (“share, part, party”), from Old French part, from Latin pars.
From Middle High German partīe, from Old French partie. Cognate with English party, Italian partita. Doublet of Partie and Party.

From Early New High German pass, from Middle High German pas (“parts of a deer's entrails”) (but also West Central German "step, walk, gait, way", also "the right measure; the right, appropriate time" by influence of Middle Dutch, whence Late Middle High German pas (“"measured part, section”), compa
Relatinization of Middle High German fēnix, fēnichs, fēnīs, themselves (in part through Old French fenix) from Latin phoenix, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix).
From Middle High German bensel, pensel, from Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin pēnicellus, alteration of Latin pēnicillum (“brush”).
Inherited from Middle High German birsen, from Old French berser.

From Middle High German plaz, from Old French place, from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Cognate with English place. Displaced native Old High German zīh (“place, court/village square, market”).
From Middle High German polieren, which is borrowed from Old French polir (see modern French polir).
From Middle High German pomp(e) f (13th c.), from Old French pompe and directly from its source, Latin pompa, which see. Masculine use began in the 15th century and established itself by the 18th.
From Middle High German port, borrowed from Old French port, itself borrowed from Latin portus (“harbor”).
From Middle High German busūne, busīne, from Old French buisine, from Latin būcina, with a change to stress on the last syllable (influenced by the suffix -īnus).

From Middle High German posse (“prank, farce”), from Old French bosse (“bump, lump, swelling, sublimity, loftiness”), from Vulgar Latin *bottia, from Frankish *bottija, from Frankish *bōtan (“to strike, knock down”), from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to beat, push”).

From Middle High German prīsen (“to praise”), a derivative of the noun prīs (“prize”) (whence modern German Preis), influenced by Old French prisier (“to appraise, value”), from Late Latin pretiō (“to esteem, value”).

From Middle High German priester, from Old High German priester, borrowed around 700 (after the High German consonant shift, but before the diphthongisation of West Germanic ē) from pre-Old French prestre, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Doublet of Presbyter. Imme
From Old French prince, from Latin prīnceps (“first head”), from prīmus (“first”) + capere (“seize, take”).

parole.significato: in good condition: clean; neat; well-kept; developed
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old French propre, from Latin proprius. Probably borrowed in north-western dialects via Middle Dutch proper [13th c., sense: 15th c.], later generalized under the influence of modern French propre. The colloquial euphemism for “chubby” may, in part, be due to association with Proppen

From Middle High German prophēzīen, derived from prophēzīe, a byform of prophētīe (see Prophetie). The z-form was influenced by Old French profecie. The verb itself may also follow Old French profecier (whence at any rate Middle High German prophēzieren).
From Middle High German prob(e)st, brobest, from Old High German probost, probist, provost, from Old French provost, from Latin praepositus.

parole.significato: gift, present (something given to another voluntarily, without charge)
parole.testo: From Middle High German prēsent, prīsant, from Old French present.
Inherited from Middle High German prēsentieren, borrowed from Old French présenter. Cognate with French présenter.

From Middle High German povel, bovel (“folk, people”, ca. 1200). Generally derived from Old French pueble, pueple. However, since Middle High German consistently shows -v-, borrowing from Italian Gallo-Romance povolo should also be considered. In any case from Latin populus. The form with -b- shows
Derived from Old French purer, from Late Latin purare (“to clean”).
From Old French queste, from Latin quaesīta.
From Middle High German regieren, borrowed from Old French reger, from Latin regō. Cognate with Hunsrik rëghiere.
Borrowed in the 19th century from Middle High German reige, an alternative form of reie, itself perhaps a borrowing of Old French raie; replaced inherited Reihen.
Borrowed from Old French rente, from Early Medieval Latin rendita.
From Middle High German roc, from Old French roche, ultimately from Persian رخ (rox, “rook”).
From Middle High German rollen, from Old French roeler, from Medieval Latin rotulāre, from Latin rotula.
From Middle High German rotte, from Old French rote, from Latin rupta, perfect participle of rumpo. Cognate with Middle English route, Dutch rot, English rout.

parole.significato: To form into a gang, to rout, squad.
parole.testo: From Middle High German roten, derived from rote (whence modern Rotte), from Old French rote, from Latin rupta.
From Middle High German rubrike, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rubrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

parole.significato: round, rounded, similar as in English, especially:
parole.testo: From Middle High German runt, from Old French ront, from Latin rotundus (“round”) from rota (“wheel, disk”).
From Middle High German sāne, from Old French sain, saime, from Latin sagīna (“nourishment”), of uncertain origin. Compare Middle Low German sān, sāne, saeum, from the same Old French source.

Inherited from Middle High German samīt, borrowed from Old French samit, from Medieval Latin samitum, borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἑξάμιτος (hexámitos), from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-, “six”) + μῐ́τος (mĭ́tos, “thread, strand”).
From Middle High German schalemīe (13th century); from Old French chalemie, a suffixal variant of chalemel (compare French chalumeau), from Latin calamellus.
Middle High German schecke, from Old French eschec (“check”), thus “checkered”.
Inherited from Middle High German simpel, from Old French simple.

parole.significato: standard (flag at the apex of a vertical pole)
parole.testo: From Middle High German standert or stanthart (first attested in the 13ᵗʰ century), from Old French estandart (“standard”). Doublet of Standard.
From Middle High German stivel, from Old High German stival, borrowed from Old French estivel, perhaps from Latin aestas (“summer”) or Latin stipes (“tree trunk, log”).
From Middle High German tabernakel, from Old French tabernacle, from Latin tabernāculum.

From Middle High German tanzen, from Old French dancer; the adapted onset t- in Upper German dialects (and standard German) proves that the word was not borrowed directly from the French word, but via Middle Low German or Middle Dutch dansen and Central German.

From Middle High German tartsche, from Old French targe, from Old Norse targa, from Proto-Germanic *targǭ. Compare cognate Old High German zarga, whence modern Zarge (“frame”), Old English targe, whereas Middle Low German tartze, tartzge and Middle Dutch tarche, tartse are also borrowings from Old F
From Middle High German test (“melting pot”), from Old French test, from Latin testum.
From Middle High German thrōn, trōn, from Old French tron, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “seat, place of honour”).

Inherited by the late 12th century (Hartmann von Aue) from Middle High German tjost f, tjoste f, jiust f, jiuste f, joste f, schust f, but also (more rarely) as tust m, just m, just m, gust m, tschuscht m. From Old French jouster. Cognate with English joust.

From Middle High German trëse, from Old High German trëso (“treasure, treasury”), from Old French tresor, which see. Originally referred to a cash box, then shifting to the desk on which such a box would be situated. Doublet of Tresor and Thesaurus.
From Old French trompe (“trumpet”). |

parole.significato: baggage train (a unit’s supply vehicles and the troops resonsible for them)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German trosse (“baggage”), from Old French trosse, trousse (“package, bundle”). The semantic development from “baggage” to “those who move the baggage” occurred around 1500. Cognate with English truss, which see.

parole.significato: tower, spire (very tall building or structure, especially with a tapering top)
parole.testo: From Middle High German turm, an East Central German variant of turn, from Old High German turn, from Old French *torn (cf. the diminutive tornele), variant of tor, from Latin turris. From the same Old French source are Dutch toren, Low German Toorn. The final -m is probably due to sporadic dissimil

From Late Middle High German turnier, alteration (after the verb turnieren) of older turnei, tornei, from Old French tornoi, itself deverbal from Old French tornoiier, tornier (“to turn, romp, fight in a tournament”), from torner (“to turn”), from Latin tornare (“to turn”).

parole.significato: vassal, leud, feudal tenant (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vassal, from Old French vassal.

From Middle High German wambes, wambeis, from Old French wambais, from Medieval Latin wambāsium, bambāsium. This is predominantly considered a derivative of Frankish *wamba, from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“belly, womb”), making Wams a doublet of Wamme (“dewlap”) and Wampe (“potbelly, paunch”). Alternat
From Middle High German cē̆ment, byform of more common cī̆ment(e), z-, from Old French ciment, cement, from Latin caementum.
From late Middle High German zifer (“digit”), from Old French cifre, from Medieval Latin cifra, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr).
From Middle High German zinober, from Old French cinobre, from Latin cinnabaris, from Ancient Greek κιννάβαρι (kinnábari).
